newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian stocks end 1996 at record levels.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian stocks end 1996 at record levels.

text.p: SPI 2424.80 +4.80 US 30yr cl 6.54 unch
10yrbond futs 92.520 -0.020 Gold NY 369.40 Lon Fix 369.60
*Stocks end holiday-shortened session and 1996 at record closing level. Volumes light. Volume 195.2 million, value A$423.32 million, 970 stocks traded, 323 steady, 418 rises, 229 falls
Australian shares closed at record levels on Tuesday in a holiday-shortened session where the few brokers on deck put a positive spin on the last day of 1996.

At 1.00 p.m. (0200 GMT), the All Ordinaries index was 11.7 points up at 2,424.6 after reaching an record intraday high of 2426.5, surpassing the previous record high of 2416.8 set on December 30. December share price index futures were 4.8 points up at 2,424.8, a 0.2 point premium to the underlying index.
While end of year window-dressing and futures-led buying as the December SPI contract closed out provided most of the momentum, broker said the overall tone was one of confidence.

"The U.S. seems to be a significant factor in recent times. The fact that they went down but then bounced up has given us a bit more confidence that there won't be a correction," said analyst David Perry of Austock Brokers, adding that interest in the resource leaders had boosted sentiment in the last two days.
"The resources stocks have been up a bit and there is a bit of interest creeping back into that area."
While Perry noted portfolio shuffling as the year ended was occurring, the level remained difficult to quantify.
"There is some speculative end of year activity but I'm not sure how much there is," he said.
Over the calendar year, the All Ordinaries index rose 10.1 percent compared with a 15.2 percent rise in calendar 1995.

The industrial sector easily outperformed the resources sector during the year with the All Industrials index rising 14.3 percent to 3,754.9 while the All Resources index only rose 1.4 percent to 1,406.2.
The market's rise occurred despite a fall by Australia's largest company, BHP, whose shares finished the year at A$17.92, A$1.08 or 5.7 percent lower than its 1995 close of A$19.00.
BHP has faced lower profits, especially from its expensive U.S. copper operations.

Catching trader's eyes on the last day of 1996 was Papuan New Guinea mining investor, Orogen Minerals, which continued its recent strong rise as investors sought exposure to the PNG resource sector. Since listing on November 1, 1996, its shares have risen 43 percent.
Rises outnumbered falls by a ratio of about nine to five, while about 33 percent of stocks traded remained steady.
FUTURES/OPTIONS - Futures was light after several days of solid activity while options trade was slow.
Total options traded 18,721 (17,941)
Turnover in December SPI contracts totalled 3,414 (8,481)

In other local markets, the Australian bond market's generally bullish year ended in a bit of an anti-climax with futures prices marginally softer on the day and the turnover seasonally light. The softer bias reflected a fairly inactive U.S. Treasury market which gave up the gains seen in overseas trading on Monday and a holiday in Japan. By 12.30 p.m. (0130 GMT), 10 year T-bonds were yielding 7.39 percent.

The Australian dollar remained comfortably cradled in its recent tight range Tuesday as the local market wound down early for the New Year holiday. By 12.30 p.m. (0130 GMT), the unit was reclining at US$0.7976/71 having wandered up from US$0.7957/62.
